definition: Recalcitrant means stubbornly defiant of authority or control.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word recalcitrant. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know recalcitrant should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Two detentions later, the recalcitrant sophomore still wore the hat, offering no reason beyond a level stare.

Unwilling is far milder than recalcitrant — a student who would rather not clean the lab may still pick up the sponge without a word, while a recalcitrant student digs in and defies the instruction itself.
Resistant goes further than unwilling — feet drag, objections get raised — but it stops short of recalcitrant, which plants itself and defies the authority outright.

Balky describes a mule, an engine, or a person that digs in against handling or direction and simply will not move on cue. Recalcitrant is narrower and more human: cold, deliberate defiance aimed at whoever holds the reins, not just a refusal to budge.

Unruly means hard to govern out of wildness or high spirits — a rowdy class, a colt that will not stand still. The disorder is overflowing energy, not a plan. Recalcitrant is colder and more deliberate: a set jaw turned against the person in charge, defiance chosen on purpose.
does as asked, without a fight
works along willingly, even helpfully

Latin calcitrare, 'to kick,' came from calx, 'heel' — and neither hoofprint survives anywhere else in everyday English. The kick lives on only inside recalcitrant itself, so learn the picture rather than hunting a cousin: heels planted, lashing back at the handler.
Recalcitrant means stubbornly defiant of authority or control.
The chess team's newest star was flatly recalcitrant: she would not play the openings her coach assigned.
Board after board she pushed her own pawns her own way, lost brilliantly or won ugly, and met every lecture about preparation with folded arms.
Nothing was wrong with her game; she had decided that nobody would steer it.
Recalcitrant is the exact word for her, because it means stubbornly defiant of authority or control — the resistance is aimed at whoever holds the reins.
Unruly comes close, but unruly suggests wildness or high spirits; recalcitrant is colder and more deliberate, a set jaw against the person in charge.
Recalcitrant is for open, dug-in defiance of whoever holds the reins — stronger than stubborn, more deliberate than unruly.
Keep it apart from three unit-mates a reader might blur together: remiss neglects a duty without defying anyone; reticent holds back words, not deeds; repentant has already surrendered and is sorry.
If the sentence needs someone kicking against authority itself, recalcitrant is the word.

In 1911 the Lighthouse Board ordered its keepers to adopt a new logbook format: one page per shift, no marginal notes.
Most stations complied within the month.
At Gull Point, keeper Elias Voss read the circular, initialed it, and went on keeping his log exactly as before.
Inspectors cited him in April and again in July.
Each citation came back with a courteous note explaining that his margins had once caught a wreck-causing error the new format would have hidden.
The Board's annual report called him recalcitrant, and the word was fair: this was no oversight but a deliberate, standing refusal of a direct instruction.
Even his supervisors conceded the defiance was principled, since his log remained the most accurate on the coast.
